records.title: Commercialization control: DM-IMP evidence → IP → licensing → royalties
records.body:
## Objective
Convert the Dr Moagi Intelligence Media Processor from an operational reference architecture into a defensible, benchmarked, licensable processor-IP package without making unverified SOTA claims.

## Control law
Working → Robust → Portable → Elegant → Advanced.

No commercial claim advances unless its evidence gate is satisfied. No adaptive/runtime claim is promoted from proposed to verified without reproducible measurements.

## Workstreams
- [ ] #177 — IP/provenance, prior art and claim families
- [ ] #178 — reproducible SOTA benchmark harness
- [ ] #179 — FPGA/RTL timing and resource proof
- [ ] #180 — codec-aware image/audio/video adapters
- [ ] #181 — formal semantics, fuzzing and crash consistency
- [ ] #182 — licensing package, royalty model and design-win pipeline

## Dependency graph
```text
                 #177 IP / claim map
                        |
        +---------------+----------------+
        |                                |
        v                                v
 #178 SOTA evidence                #181 verification
        |                                |
        +------------+-------------------+
                     |
                     v
              #179 hardware proof
                     |
                     v
              #180 media adapters
                     |
                     v
              #182 licensing / design wins
```

Workstreams may execute in parallel, but external performance claims require #178 evidence; hardware timing claims require #179; patentability assertions require counsel review of #177; production licensing requires satisfactory #181 diligence.

## Primary promotion gates
1. Counsel-ready invention/disclosure package exists.
2. A third party can reproduce benchmark evidence.
3. Hardware implementation produces post-route timing/resource evidence.
4. Image/audio/video outputs are codec-valid with separated quality loss.
5. Bytecode/runtime security and rollback properties have reproducible verification/fuzz evidence.
6. Evaluation package and royalty structure are commercially reviewable.
7. First qualified licensee reproduces the evaluation and enters a design-in/commercial process.

## Current technical anchor
Mainline DM-IMP merge: `62d0cd8e0cfb28e452645a86fa43de709004a416`.

## Commercial principle
Retain ownership; prefer field-of-use licensing with measurable milestones, auditability and minimum commitments over broad assignment/exclusivity.

## Definition of 'beyond SOTA'
A claim is permitted only for a named metric, workload, baseline, hardware/software configuration and reproducible result. 'Beyond SOTA' is not a global label for the architecture.

This issue is the orchestration control plane.

records.title: [Perf]: list_sessions_rich re-walks compression chains N+1 per row under the global write lock — redundant with its own recursive CTE
records.body:
## Summary

`SessionDB.list_sessions_rich()` resolves compression-chain tips **twice**: its SQL already walks every chain via a recursive CTE, then a Python loop re-walks the identical edges hop-by-hop — one query **and one acquisition of the store's global write lock per hop per row** (`hermes_state.py:10155-10167`):

```python
if project_compression_tips and not include_children:
    tip_ids_by_root: Dict[str, str] = {}
    for s in sessions:
        if s.get("end_reason") != "compression":
            continue
        tip_id = self.get_compression_tip(s["id"])   # N+1 walk
        if tip_id != s["id"]:
            tip_ids_by_root[s["id"]] = tip_id
```

and `get_compression_tip()` takes `self._lock` around every hop (`hermes_state.py:9751-9776`):

```python
for _ in range(100):
    with self._lock:                                  # writer lock, per hop
        cursor = self._conn.execute("""
            SELECT child.id FROM sessions parent
            JOIN sessions child ON child.parent_session_id = parent.id
            WHERE parent.id = ? AND parent.end_reason = 'compression' ...
```

When `order_by_last_active=True`, the same method has *already* resolved the exact same chains in one statement via `WITH RECURSIVE chain(root_id, cur_id)` + `chain_max` (`hermes_state.py:10037-10055`) — the Python block re-computes what the CTE just produced. The in-code comment ("per-session graph walk, not batchable in one query", :10156-10158) predates the CTE and is no longer true on that path.

## Why it matters

- Cost is **R×D extra queries + R×D lock acquisitions** per listing (R = compression roots on the page, D = average chain depth). Compression runs automatically at ~50% context, so on long-lived installs most old conversations are roots; a 20-50-row page means dozens of locked round-trips per refresh.
- The lock taken is the store's **global** lock shared with writers — sidebar reads serialize against concurrent message appends and token flushes. Users see the picker/sessions list hitch exactly while another conversation is actively writing.
- Hot path: desktop/API session listing passes `order_by_last_active=True` with default `project_compression_tips=True` (`gateway/platforms/api_server.py:4256, 4285`), the `/resume` picker (`hermes_cli/session_listing.py:77`), console engine (`hermes_cli/console_engine.py:1348`), dashboard session routers.

## Symptom

Sessions-list / resume-picker latency grows linearly with how much history has been compressed; periodic multi-hundred-ms stalls when any session is mid-write. Worst on multi-month heavy installs.

## Suggested fix

Project tip ids out of the existing `chain`/`chain_max` CTE into the outer SELECT (they're already computed there), or resolve them in one batched follow-up statement keyed by the page's root ids — replacing the per-row `get_compression_tip()` loop entirely. At minimum, route `get_compression_tip()` reads through `_read_ctx()` (WAL reader pool) instead of `self._lock` so listings stop contending with writers.

records.title: [AUTOPILOT05] Persistent five-lane Work loop
records.body:
Purpose: replace high-churn one-off chat bursts with five persistent, independently self-refreshing Work lanes. This issue is a coordination surface only; it does not replace locked Drive governance, canonical ownership, AUDIT01/AUDIT02, or production gates.

Why: BURST01/BURST02 proved high fan-out improves discovery but also creates stale-branch review, duplicate QA and CI contention. External batch-runner evidence from a separate project showed a 10-tabs-per-minute model produced only 29 confirmed sends out of 101 targets, with 46 send-button failures before the later rate/usage pause. AUTOPILOT05 therefore uses five long-lived chats, staggered starts, one new work pulse only after a lane finishes, and rotation after 20 successful work pulses in a chat.

Five stable lanes:
1. CANONICAL CONVERGENCE — sole writer of PR #9 / work3/integration-release-candidate. Integrates reviewed current specialist slices, preserves provenance, stabilizes exact SHA, runs exact canonical gates. If exact-head CI is running/queued, do not churn the head merely to stay busy; analyze next integration and current blockers instead.
2. RUNTIME / RELEASE / HOSTIQ — owns non-live runtime, deployment/recovery, Passenger, PREPARE, schema migration/rollback and candidate-bound production-evidence preparation. No live deploy/restart without independent authorization.
3. TELEGRAM PRODUCT / TELETHON — owns read/search/dialog continuation, marked peer IDs, media/download/ZIP, write semantics, SEND_FILES composition, strict API/OpenAPI parity and real Telethon 1.44 semantics on isolated specialist lines.
4. RELIABILITY / SECURITY / ADVERSARIAL — owns SQLite multi-process state, exactly-once crash behavior, locks/TOCTOU, secret/workflow/session security, fuzz/fault injection, performance/retention defects. Isolated fixes/tests only; no competing canonical writer.
5. INDEPENDENT AUDIT / QA / COMPLETION — read-only product audit by default. Reconstructs exact state, falsifies developer claims, maintains residual-gap and integration priority map, acceptance truth, stale/duplicate PR classification and production gate. Never silently becomes canonical developer.

Per-cycle protocol for every lane:
- Fresh-read mandatory Drive governance and current GitHub state before deciding work. Live GitHub code/PR/CI wins over stale prose.
- Read this issue plus #62, #35 and relevant permanent role/audit issues.
- Inspect the lane's most recent checkpoint and actual current branches/PRs; do not redo completed work.
- Select the largest safe high-value task that materially advances final PASS. If the nominal task is already solved, pivot within the same lane to the highest residual gap.
- Work deeply in Work mode. Do not stop after one finding/test if further safe lane-owned work remains.
- Post exact branch/PR/SHA/CI/findings/next state here and to the relevant permanent issue.
- Missing/stale checkpoints never freeze progress; reconstruct facts directly.

Rotation protocol:
- Each physical chat belongs permanently to one lane slot. Slot mapping by chat number: lane1 = 1,6,11,16...; lane2 = 2,7,12,17...; lane3 = 3,8,13,18...; lane4 = 4,9,14,19...; lane5 = 5,10,15,20....
- After 20 successful work prompts in a physical chat, retire that chat. Open the next chat for the same slot and use the lane rotation bootstrap; it must reconstruct from GitHub/Drive/this issue, not depend on old chat memory.
- If multiple chats retire together, create replacements staggered by 3–5 minutes.
- Duplicate/repeated prompt delivery is safe by design: before acting, the lane checks the latest checkpoint/current state and continues from there rather than repeating already-completed work.

Safety remains absolute: public repo, no secrets/private Telegram content; no merge/deploy/Passenger restart/live Telegram operation/K5/credential request without applicable independent gate. USER_TELEGRAM_AUTH_NOT_YET_REQUIRED remains authoritative until validated release/runtime evidence makes Telegram auth the first genuine human blocker.

Current starting convergence facts must always be re-read live. At creation, canonical PR #9 is still OPEN/DRAFT/NOT MERGED at 84691967e5363bc4b88dfae97371d7bf329c105d; BURST02 showed useful specialist/audit work but no newer canonical commit. Treat that SHA only as the creation-time anchor, not a permanent truth.

records.title: [11] Coordinator mode — assembled from parts, not built
records.body:
> **Parity row 11** · kandev: *Coordinator mode — have an agent coordinate sub-tasks executed by other agents* (roadmap, **Done**)

**Blocked by #56** (sub-tasks), **#6** (task dependencies), **#99** (MCP: create tasks and subtasks)

## Context

This issue exists mainly to record a **decision not to build something**.

"Coordinator mode" reads like a feature needing an orchestration engine, a planner, and a delegation protocol. It is not. It is an emergent property of three capabilities that are each worth building on their own merits:

| Capability | Issue |
|---|---|
| Create sub-tasks that inherit context | #56 + #99 |
| Declare dependencies so children run in order | #6 + row 79 |
| Record a plan and signal step completion | row 85 + row 86 |

An agent with those tools **is** a coordinator. Building a bespoke coordinator first creates a second orchestration path that workflows (#5) will later contradict, and the contradiction surfaces as unexplainable board behaviour.

## Proposed implementation

Almost nothing new:

1. An agent-profile flag marking a profile as coordinator-capable, which simply grants the broader MCP scope (create sub-tasks, message siblings) that row 75's default task-scoped token withholds.
2. A **delegation depth bound** and a **total-subtask bound** per root Task. Recursive decomposition without a bound is how one prompt becomes two hundred agent runs; row 61's concurrency cap limits parallelism but not total volume.
3. A coordinator's own Task is subject to the same review gate as any other (Principle I).

If this issue turns out to need more than that, the prerequisite features are wrong and should be fixed there.

## Second-order effects

- **Depends on:** #56, #6, #99, and rows 79, 85, 86
- **Requires no new orchestration engine** — that is the point
- **Bounded by:** row 61 (parallelism) and this issue's depth bound (volume)

## UI

A "coordinator" `Switch` on the Agent Profile with a plain statement of the extra authority it grants. In the task workspace, a delegation tree showing children and their states, reusing #56's Subtasks section.

**Components** — `existing` Card, Badge, TaskCard · **new** Switch, Collapsible (shared with #56)

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] AC-1: THE SYSTEM SHALL let an Agent Profile be marked coordinator-capable, granting sub-task creation and sibling messaging scope.
- [ ] AC-2: THE SYSTEM SHALL enforce a maximum delegation depth and a maximum total sub-task count per root Task.
- [ ] AC-3: THE SYSTEM SHALL apply the review gate to a coordinator's own changes as to any other Task (Principle I).
- [ ] AC-4: THE SYSTEM SHALL show the delegation tree with each descendant's state.
- [ ] AC-5: THE SYSTEM SHALL introduce no orchestration path other than the existing durable workflow.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] `make verify` exits 0
- [ ] Tests: depth and volume bounds enforced; scope granted only to coordinator profiles (Principle VI)
- [ ] Grep gate: no second orchestration entry point
- [ ] `docs/features/F04-agent-orchestration.md` updated

## References

- kandev: [Roadmap — Coordinator mode](https://github.com/kdlbs/kandev/blob/main/docs/roadmap.md)

records.title: [build-timings] Build Performance Report — 2026-08-28
records.body:
## Build Summary

- **Total build time**: 2m 17s (wall clock, `cargo build --workspace --timings`, clean state)
- **Compilation units**: 372
- **Max concurrency**: high in the first ~90s (dozens of small proc-macro/leaf crates), then narrows sharply as the build serializes on `rustls` → `hyper-rustls` → `reqwest` → `jsonschema` → `libaipm-engine-spec` (build script) → `libaipm` → `aipm`
- **Compiler**: `rustc 1.98.0 (88d9e12ae 2026-08-18)`, `cargo 1.98.0`

## Top 5 Slowest Compilation Units

| Crate | Duration | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `aws-lc-sys` 0.40.0 | 59.7s | `run-custom-build` — compiles the AWS-LC C/assembly crypto library |
| `libgit2-sys` 0.17.0+1.8.1 | 50.4s | `run-custom-build` — compiles vendored libgit2 C sources |
| `syn` 2.0.117 | 16.3s | proc-macro dependency, pulled in transitively many times |
| `rustls` 0.23.37 | 14.5s / 13.5s (two builds, different feature sets) | pulled in via both `reqwest`'s TLS stack and `jsonschema`'s `resolve-http` feature |
| `jsonschema` 0.46.4 | 13.6s | default features pull in `reqwest` + `rustls` + `aws-lc-rs` |
| `reqwest` 0.13.3 | 11.5s | full HTTP client stack, only used transitively for `jsonschema`'s HTTP `$ref` resolution |

These six units alone account for **~166s of single-threaded compile time**, and they sit on the critical path feeding into `libaipm-engine-spec`'s **build script**, which nothing else can start until it finishes — this is the primary bottleneck.

## Dependency Analysis

- `cargo tree --duplicates` shows **15 crate names** with 2+ versions in the dependency graph, most notably:
  - `thiserror` 1.0.69 (via `gherkin`, a cucumber test dep) **and** 2.0.18 (workspace-used) — two full macro/impl compilations
  - `tower` 0.4.13 (`tower-lsp`) and 0.5.3 (`reqwest`)
  - `bitflags` 1.3.2 / 2.11.0, `getrandom` 0.2/0.3/0.4, `hashbrown` 0.14/0.16, `heck` 0.4/0.5, `regex-syntax` 0.7/0.8, `openssl-probe` 0.1/0.2
  - None of these are within direct control (all come from transitive deps of `cucumber`, `assert_cmd`, `git2`, `jsonschema`), but they add duplicate compile work per version.
- The single largest avoidable cost is that **`jsonschema` is pulled in with its default features**, which enable `resolve-http` (→ `reqwest`, `rustls`, `aws-lc-rs`, `hyper-rustls`, `tokio-rustls`, `rustls-platform-verifier`) and `tls-aws-lc-rs` (→ `aws-lc-sys`, a slow C/asm build). `crates/libaipm-engine-spec/build.rs` only calls `jsonschema::validator_for(&meta_schema)` to validate a **local, already-embedded** schema file (`data/engine-api-schema.json` against the committed meta-schema) — it never fetches a schema over HTTP. The HTTP/TLS resolution stack pulled in by the default features (`resolve-http`, `tls-aws-lc-rs`) is dead weight for this build-script use case.
- `libgit2-sys`'s native build (50s) is required by `git2`, used in `libaipm` for repo operations — not easily avoidable without dropping `git2`, but it is a one-time cost cached by `Swatinem/rust-cache` in CI.

## Cargo Lint Findings

- `cargo clippy --workspace -- -D warnings`: **zero warnings**, clean pass in 1m12s (warm cache).
- `[workspace.lints.clippy]` already enables the `cargo` lint group (`warn`) plus `all`/`pedantic`/`perf` (`deny`) — no further lint-group changes needed.
- `[profile.dev.package."*"]` already sets `opt-level = 1` for third-party deps (good — keeps native/C-heavy deps like `libgit2-sys`/`aws-lc-sys` fast at runtime after first build) while workspace crates (`libaipm`, `aipm`) stay at `opt-level = 0` for fast iteration. This is already well-tuned.

## Recommendations

1. **[High impact]** Disable `jsonschema`'s default features and select only what's needed for local/offline validation. In `Cargo.toml`, change:
   ```toml
   jsonschema = "0.46"
   ```
   to:
   ```toml
   jsonschema = { version = "0.46", default-features = false, features = ["resolve-file"] }
   ```
   (or no extra features at all if `$ref`s in the meta-schema never resolve external file/HTTP references). This removes `reqwest`, `rustls`, `hyper-rustls`, `tokio-rustls`, `rustls-platform-verifier`, and `aws-lc-rs`/`aws-lc-sys` (the single slowest unit at 59.7s) from the build graph entirely if the build script doesn't need HTTP/file resolution — verify with `cargo build -p libaipm-engine-spec` after the change and re-run the schema-drift test (`tests/schema_export_drift.rs`). Estimated savings: **60–90s** off a clean build, and removes ~8-10 crates from the dependency count.
2. **[Medium impact]** If any TLS resolution is genuinely required, prefer `tls-ring` over the default `tls-aws-lc-rs` — `ring`'s crypto is typically faster to compile than `aws-lc-sys`'s C/assembly build on cold cache, though `aws-lc-sys` benefits more from caching once built.
3. **[Low impact]** The duplicate `thiserror` 1.x/2.x versions stem from `gherkin` (a transitive dep of the `cucumber` BDD test framework) still pinning `thiserror` 1.x while the rest of the workspace uses 2.x. No workspace-level fix is available since this is upstream in `gherkin`; safe to ignore, adds only marginal duplicate-compile cost in test builds.
4. **[Low impact]** `tower` 0.4 (via `tower-lsp`) vs `tower` 0.5 (via `reqwest`) is likewise upstream-driven (no compatible `tower-lsp` release using `tower` 0.5 at this time) — no action recommended.
5. No unused-dependency issues were found; `cargo clippy`'s `cargo` lint group (already enabled at `warn`) did not flag any `multiple_crate_versions`-style or unused-dep issues beyond what's listed above.

## Trend

No prior `build-timings` issues were found in the repository to compare against — this is the first report of its kind. Future runs should compare total build time and the top-5 slowest units against these baseline numbers (2m17s total; `aws-lc-sys` 59.7s and `libgit2-sys` 50.4s as the two dominant single units).

records.title: Add Kahn's algorithm for topological sorting
records.body:
## Summary

Graaf only implements DFS-based topological sorting. Kahn's algorithm (the BFS/in-degree-based alternative) is not implemented.

## Current state

`include/graaflib/algorithm/topological_sorting/` contains only `dfs_topological_sorting.h`/`.tpp`. There is a related historical request, [#114 "[ALGO] Kahn's Algorithm"](../issues/114), which was closed without being implemented (closed due to inactivity, not as "won't do").

## Why this matters

Kahn's algorithm is the standard alternative to DFS-based topological sorting, and it has properties the DFS version doesn't: it naturally detects cycles as a side effect (if not all vertices are output, the graph has a cycle), it processes vertices in in-degree order rather than via recursion (avoiding recursion-depth concerns on very large or deep graphs), and it more naturally supports "level" or "layer" based processing where all vertices at the same dependency depth are grouped together. Offering only one of the two standard approaches leaves a well-known, commonly requested gap for anyone whose use case wants those specific properties (e.g. build-system dependency ordering, layered scheduling).

## Suggested resolution

- Implement Kahn's algorithm (in-degree-based, using a queue) alongside the existing DFS-based version under `include/graaflib/algorithm/topological_sorting/`.
- Reuse existing `vertex_properties::vertex_indegree` where convenient.
- Add corresponding documentation under `docs/docs/algorithms/topological-sort/`, including complexity and how it compares to the existing DFS-based approach.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Kahn's algorithm is implemented for directed graphs.
- [ ] It detects and reports cycles (e.g. via the same mechanism/exception used elsewhere in the library, such as in `bellman_ford`'s negative-cycle detection).
- [ ] Documentation added, including complexity and a comparison with the existing DFS-based approach.
- [ ] Unit tests cover DAGs, cyclic graphs, and disconnected graphs.

records.title: feat(permissions): Implement hierarchical ACL checking engine with Redis caching layer
records.body:
Description
Design and develop a hierarchical permission/ACL evaluation engine where document access rights can be inherited from parent collections (directories/folders) or groups, utilizing a Redis caching layer to bypass heavy DB joins on hot paths.

Context
Contracts and company documents are organized into folders. Permission grants can occur at the individual document level, the parent directory level, or the group membership level. Fetching and validating this tree structures on every API request introduces heavy performance penalties.

Technical Implementation Blueprint
Hierarchical Resolution Logic: Write a recursive database utility or common table expression (CTE) query to resolve the effective access level for a user:
sql:
WITH RECURSIVE folder_path AS (
    SELECT id, parent_id, id as origin_id FROM folders WHERE id = :target_folder_id
    UNION ALL
    SELECT f.id, f.parent_id, p.origin_id FROM folders f
    INNER JOIN folder_path p ON f.id = p.parent_id
)
SELECT permission FROM acl 
WHERE (object_id IN (SELECT id FROM folder_path) OR object_id = :document_id)
  AND (subject_id = :user_id OR subject_id IN (SELECT group_id FROM user_groups WHERE user_id = :user_id))
ORDER BY priority DESC LIMIT 1;

Redis Permission Caching: Cache resolved keys in Redis: user:permissions:{tenant_id}:{user_id}:{document_id} string containing the resolved access level (READ, WRITE, ADMIN, NONE).
Invalidation Listeners: Add SQLAlchemy event listeners on ACL and UserGroup models to invalidate relevant Redis keys when permissions are modified.
Acceptance Criteria
 Access control correctly respects group membership and directory inheritance hierarchy.
 Permission check overhead must not exceed 5ms for cached values.
 Modifying folder permissions instantly invalidates the cache for all documents contained recursively inside it.

records.title: C backend: a self-referencing struct cannot be ordered, only forward-declared (24 specs)
records.body:
## The defect

C requires a type's name before any use of it. The C backend emitted every struct
as an anonymous typedef:

```c
typedef struct {
    BTreeNode** children;      /* BTreeNode is not in scope */
    K* keys;
} BTreeNode;                   /* ...until this line closes */
```

A struct that names itself is a **cycle of length one**. The topological sort
landed in #2941 orders declarations by dependency, and no ordering can put a
declaration before itself — the sort is powerless here by construction, not by
oversight.

**Measured: 24 corpus specs write a self-referencing struct.**

## The fix

Emit a forward-declaration block, then tagged bodies:

```c
typedef struct BTreeNode BTreeNode;   /* names the tag */

struct BTreeNode { ... };             /* tagged, so the name above refers to it */
```

An anonymous `typedef struct { ... } Name;` cannot be forward-declared at all —
there is no tag to declare — so the body had to become tagged for the forward
declaration to mean anything. The two changes are one change.

The topological sort stays: a forward declaration gives C the **name**, which is
enough for a pointer member and *not* enough for a by-value member. The two
mechanisms cover different halves of the same requirement, and a mutant that
disables the sort is still killed by its own tests (M4 below).

## Measurement

Per spec, both directions, on an idle machine, 650 corpus specs:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `cc -fsyntax-only -std=gnu11` accepts | 264 | **268** |

- **newly accepted: 4** — `encoding/markup`, `trees/b_tree`, `trees/kd_tree`, `trees/rtree`
- **regressions: 0** (empty set, computed as `before - after`)

All four are tree structures — the family the defect was found in. This is a
small number against 24 carrying specs, and the honest reading is that the other
20 are blocked further down; `b_tree` itself still fails on `BTreeNode(K, V)*
children` — a **generic-parameterised type name reaching C**, which has no
generics. That is a separate defect and it is not fixed here.

## Mutation testing

Four mutants, each killed by the test that should catch it:

| mutant | killed by |
|---|---|
| M1 drop the forward-declaration block | `a_self_referencing_struct_is_forward_declared` |
| M2 restore the anonymous typedef body | 8 of 9 tests |
| M3 forward-declare only self-referencing structs | `every_struct_is_forward_declared_not_only_the_recursive_ones` |
| M4 (control) disable the topological sort | `a_struct_used_before_it_is_declared_is_emitted_first` |

M3 is the interesting one: declaring only the *recursive* structs leaves a mutual
pointer cycle (`L` names `R`, `R` names `L`) with no name in scope for either.

### A mutant the freeze rejects is not a measurement

The first three mutation runs printed nothing and I nearly read that as "killed".
They were rejected by the **M5 freeze build script** — `bootstrap/stage0/FROZEN_HASH`
no longer matched — so `cargo test` never built, never ran, and produced neither a
`test result` line nor a plain `error:` line. Absence of "ok" is not death.
Mutating `compiler.rs` requires resealing `FROZEN_HASH` per mutant, and the verdict
has to separate three outcomes, not two.

## A flaky test found on the way

`bootstrap/tests/struct_order_c.rs` keyed its temp directory by
`(pid, src.len())` and each test `remove_dir_all`s it. Two tests whose sources
happen to be the same length shared one directory; under the default parallel
runner one erased the spec another was mid-read of, `t27c` printed nothing, and
the assertion read `got []`. It passed the first time it ran. Now keyed by an
atomic counter; 3 consecutive runs green.

## Seals

`tri seals drift` is **0 on master** and **356 with this change** — the C output
shape changed for every spec containing a struct, which is exactly what this
change does. 334 seal files rewritten in the same commit as the emitter and the
`FROZEN_HASH` reseal, so no commit in this branch leaves the tree inconsistent.

records.title: jq: recursive-enum printers lack the mutual-recursion refusal ordered() gives defs
records.body:
From the issue-94 landing review. `emit_jq.rs`'s new `printers()` emits one `def tl_show_X`
per printed recursive enum in DFS-discovery order, with no cycle handling -- unlike function
emission, which runs through `ordered()` and refuses a real cycle cleanly (#79). Two enums
that reference each other through Vec (`enum A { a(Vec<B>) }`, `enum B { b(Vec<A>) }`)
type-check legally; if both are printed on the jq backend, one printer references the other
before it exists and jq fails with its own raw error instead of toylang's clean refusal.

Fix: run printer defs through the same topological-sort-or-refuse path, and add a corpus or
backend_jq case pinning whichever behavior is chosen.

records.title: [EVAL:RECOVERY] Make blob reconstruction interruption-safe and descendant-clean
